subtopic_detail: Six months of lightheadedness and fatigue on standing in a fifteen year old with a sustained rise in heart rate and no fall in blood pressure
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a fifteen year old girl who has missed twenty days of school this term. For six months she has felt lightheaded and her heart has pounded within a minute or two of getting out of bed or standing in the school assembly line, and she has to sit on the floor until it passes.

She is worst in the mornings and after hot showers, is exhausted by the afternoon, and had a glandular fever like illness last summer. She has never lost consciousness, and she has no chest pain or palpitations while swimming, which she still does twice a week. Her periods are regular and not heavy, and her family history includes no sudden cardiac death or inherited heart disease.

data_table.Vital signs: Supine pulse rate 74 beats per minute, supine blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Ten minute active stand test with pulse rate rising to 118 beats per minute by eight minutes and blood pressure 116/74 mmHg at that time, no pallor or sweating during the test, heart sounds dual with no murmur on lying or standing, chest clear, no goitre, no joint hypermobility beyond the expected range, neurological examination normal
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, iron studies with ferritin 42 micrograms/L (15 to 200), thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, electrocardiogram showing sinus rhythm with normal axis, normal PR interval and corrected QT interval 410 milliseconds

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Refer her for a tilt table study and withhold any treatment advice until the result of that study is available
options.rationale: A bedside active stand test with a sustained heart rate rise of at least forty beats per minute in an adolescent already establishes the haemodynamic pattern, so tilt testing adds cost and delay without changing the first treatment step. Tilt testing is reserved for diagnostic uncertainty or for suspected reflex syncope with an unclear history. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome

options.text: Commence oral fludrocortisone daily and arrange a review of her blood pressure and electrolytes in two weeks
options.rationale: Fludrocortisone is a second line option for those who remain disabled despite a properly conducted non drug program, and it requires monitoring for hypokalaemia and hypertension. Starting it before fluid, salt and exercise measures have been tried skips the intervention with the best evidence. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome

options.text: Commence a low dose beta blocker daily and arrange a review of her symptom diary and pulse rate in four weeks
options.rationale: Low dose propranolol can blunt the tachycardia but frequently worsens the fatigue and exercise intolerance that dominate this girl's presentation, and it is considered only after non drug measures fail. The tachycardia is a compensatory response to reduced venous return rather than the primary problem. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome

options.text: Start a structured program of increased fluid and salt intake with graded recumbent exercise, and review in six weeks
options.rationale: Expanding plasma volume with two to three litres of fluid and generous dietary salt, combined with a progressive exercise program that begins in recumbent or seated positions such as rowing, swimming or cycling, is the first line treatment and the only intervention shown to improve function in adolescents. Graded exercise is started lying or seated because upright training initially provokes symptoms and abandonment. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome

options.text: Arrange a transthoracic echocardiogram and a 24 hour Holter monitor, and review her once both investigations are reported
options.rationale: Structural and arrhythmic investigation is driven by exertional syncope, palpitations at rest with abrupt onset and offset, a murmur, an abnormal electrocardiogram or a family history of sudden death, none of which are present here. Her symptoms are strictly postural and she exercises without difficulty, which argues against a primary cardiac cause. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Guidelines for the assessment of syncope)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Guidelines for the assessment of syncope

explanation.summary: Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome is defined by symptoms of orthostatic intolerance for at least three months together with a sustained heart rate rise of at least forty beats per minute in adolescents, or at least thirty in adults, within ten minutes of standing, in the absence of orthostatic hypotension. It commonly follows a viral illness, affects adolescent girls disproportionately, and causes substantial school absence through fatigue, brain fog, lightheadedness and exercise intolerance. The diagnosis is made at the bedside with an active stand test, with basic tests to exclude anaemia, iron deficiency and thyroid disease, and an electrocardiogram to look for conduction abnormalities. First line management is non pharmacological and multimodal: fluid loading, increased dietary salt, compression garments, avoidance of prolonged standing and hot environments, and a graded exercise program that begins in a recumbent or seated position and slowly moves upright. Medication such as fludrocortisone, midodrine or low dose beta blockade is added only when a properly delivered program has not restored function, and school liaison to permit water bottles, seating and a modified timetable is an essential part of care.
key_points: The adolescent diagnostic threshold is a sustained rise of at least forty beats per minute within ten minutes of standing without a fall in blood pressure.
A ten minute active stand test performed in the clinic is sufficient for diagnosis in a typical case.
Fluid loading, dietary salt, compression and graded recumbent exercise are first line and improve function.
Exercise is begun lying or seated because upright training initially provokes symptoms and leads to abandonment.
Exertional syncope, an abnormal electrocardiogram, a murmur or a family history of sudden death redirect to cardiac assessment.
explanation.pearls: The absence of a blood pressure fall is what separates this syndrome from orthostatic hypotension, so the stand test must record paired heart rate and blood pressure at intervals through ten minutes rather than a single reading at one minute.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome
Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Guidelines for the assessment of syncope
BMJ Best Practice: Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome

subtopic_detail: Timing of the first retinal examination in an extremely preterm infant stable on low flow oxygen at two weeks of age
stem:
You are the neonatal registrar reviewing a boy born at 27 weeks gestation weighing 890 g who is now 14 days old. He needed surfactant and three days of mechanical ventilation and is now on nasal high flow in 25 per cent oxygen, tolerating expressed breast milk feeds and gaining weight.

His mother asks when his eyes will be checked, having read that premature babies can go blind. The unit's ophthalmologist attends weekly and the nursing staff ask you to write the screening plan in the notes.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits for corrected gestational age
data_table.Examination: Active with good tone for corrected gestation, anterior fontanelle soft, chest clear on nasal high flow, abdomen soft with tolerated enteral feeds, red reflexes present bilaterally on bedside examination
data_table.Investigations: Cranial ultrasound at day 7 with no intraventricular haemorrhage, haemoglobin 142 g/L (140 to 220 for age), C reactive protein less than 5 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: When should his first retinal examination be arranged?

options.text: At 31 weeks postmenstrual age, which for this infant falls at four weeks after birth
options.rationale: Screening begins at whichever comes later of four weeks after birth and 31 weeks postmenstrual age, and for an infant born at 27 weeks both fall together at four weeks of age. Timing is set this way because sight threatening disease essentially never appears before 31 weeks postmenstrual age, while very immature infants examined too early are stressed for no diagnostic gain. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists: Guidelines for the screening of retinopathy of prematurity)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists: Guidelines for the screening of retinopathy of prematurity

options.text: Within the next 48 hours, since he required mechanical ventilation and supplemental oxygen
options.rationale: Ventilation and oxygen exposure raise the risk of disease but do not bring forward the examination, because the retina of an infant at 29 weeks postmenstrual age has not yet reached the stage at which treatable disease develops. An examination now would be uninformative and physiologically stressful. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists: Guidelines for the screening of retinopathy of prematurity)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists: Guidelines for the screening of retinopathy of prematurity

options.text: At 36 weeks postmenstrual age, when the retinal vasculature has reached the temporal periphery
options.rationale: Waiting until 36 weeks postmenstrual age risks missing the window in which aggressive posterior disease develops and requires treatment, which is typically between 32 and 36 weeks in infants of this gestation. Vascularisation of the temporal periphery is the endpoint for stopping screening, not for starting it. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists: Guidelines for the screening of retinopathy of prematurity)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists: Guidelines for the screening of retinopathy of prematurity

options.text: At discharge from the neonatal unit, with community ophthalmology follow up thereafter
options.rationale: Discharge timing is determined by feeding and respiratory maturity rather than by retinal development, so linking the examination to it produces unpredictable and often dangerously late screening. Screening continues on a set schedule regardless of where the infant is being cared for. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists: Guidelines for the screening of retinopathy of prematurity)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists: Guidelines for the screening of retinopathy of prematurity

options.text: At three months of corrected age in the outpatient clinic, unless the red reflexes become abnormal
options.rationale: Bedside red reflex testing detects media opacity such as cataract and does not detect peripheral retinal neovascularisation, so it cannot be used to defer formal screening. By three months corrected age treatable disease would already have progressed to detachment in an affected infant. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists: Guidelines for the screening of retinopathy of prematurity)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists: Guidelines for the screening of retinopathy of prematurity

explanation.summary: Retinopathy of prematurity is a vasoproliferative disorder of the incompletely vascularised retina and remains a preventable cause of childhood blindness in Australia. Screening is offered to infants born before 31 weeks gestation or weighing less than 1250 g at birth, with selective screening of larger infants who have had an unstable course. The first examination is timed to whichever is later of four weeks after birth or 31 weeks postmenstrual age, so very preterm infants are screened at four weeks of age while a more mature infant born at 30 weeks is screened at 31 weeks postmenstrual age. Examinations are then repeated at one to two week intervals depending on the zone and stage of disease, and screening stops only when the retina is fully vascularised or the disease has regressed with the risk of progression judged past. Treatment of type 1 disease, with laser photocoagulation or intravitreal anti vascular endothelial growth factor therapy, is delivered urgently within about 48 to 72 hours of diagnosis.
key_points: Screening criteria in Australia are birth before 31 weeks gestation or birthweight under 1250 g, with selective screening of sicker larger infants.
The first examination occurs at the later of four weeks postnatal age and 31 weeks postmenstrual age.
Red reflex testing detects media opacities and cannot substitute for indirect ophthalmoscopy of the peripheral retina.
Repeat intervals are set by the zone and stage found, not by the infant's clinical stability.
Treatable type 1 disease is addressed within about 48 to 72 hours of diagnosis.
explanation.pearls: The later of the two rules is what catches people out: an infant born at 24 weeks is not examined at four weeks of age when that would be 28 weeks postmenstrual age, and is instead examined once 31 weeks postmenstrual age is reached.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists: Guidelines for the screening of retinopathy of prematurity
Safer Care Victoria: Retinopathy of prematurity screening
BMJ Best Practice: Retinopathy of prematurity

subtopic_detail: Lethargy with 13 per cent weight loss and a raised sodium on day five of exclusive breastfeeding
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in the emergency department seeing a five day old girl brought in by her parents because she is sleepy and difficult to wake for feeds. She was born at 39 weeks by uncomplicated vaginal birth weighing 3400 g and is exclusively breastfed.

Her mother is a first time parent and describes cracked painful nipples with feeds lasting an hour and the baby still unsettled afterwards. There have been two wet nappies in the last 24 hours and the baby last passed a dark green stool yesterday. Today she weighs 2960 g.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 176 beats per minute, blood pressure 64/38 mmHg, respiratory rate 52 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in room air, temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Lethargic with a high pitched cry when disturbed, dry mucous membranes, sunken anterior fontanelle, doughy skin turgor over the abdomen, jaundice to the mid chest, capillary refill three seconds, no rash, anterior fontanelle not bulging, tone reduced but symmetrical
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 158 mmol/L (135 to 145), potassium 4.8 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5), urea 12.4 mmol/L (1.0 to 5.0), creatinine 68 micromol/L (20 to 60), glucose 3.6 mmol/L (2.6 to 6.0), serum bilirubin 268 micromol/L with treatment threshold for age 340 micromol/L, C reactive protein less than 5 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Give a 20 mL/kg bolus of 5 per cent glucose and then commence maintenance fluid, rechecking electrolytes in 12 hours
options.rationale: A glucose bolus delivers free water rapidly to a hypernatraemic brain and is the classic route to cerebral oedema and seizures during correction, and her glucose is normal so there is no metabolic indication for it. Where a bolus is needed for circulatory compromise it is given as isotonic sodium chloride. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on intravenous fluids)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on intravenous fluids

options.text: Arrange lactation support and formula top ups at home, with a weigh and clinical review by the midwife in 24 hours
options.rationale: Home management is appropriate for the well infant with modest weight loss and normal alertness, but this baby is lethargic with a sodium of 158 mmol/L and biochemical evidence of prerenal impairment. Feeding support is essential but must accompany admission rather than replace it. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on dehydration)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on dehydration

options.text: Admit for intravenous 0.9 per cent sodium chloride with glucose alongside feeding support, rechecking electrolytes four hourly
options.rationale: Hypernatraemic dehydration is corrected with isotonic fluid so that the fall in serum sodium is gradual, aiming for no more than about 0.5 mmol/L per hour or 10 to 12 mmol/L per day, with four hourly electrolytes to steer the rate. Admission also allows skilled lactation support, which addresses the cause and protects the breastfeeding relationship. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on dehydration)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on dehydration
Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on intravenous fluids

options.text: Admit for intensive phototherapy and intravenous fluids, with a repeat serum bilirubin measured six hours after starting
options.rationale: Her bilirubin sits well below the treatment threshold for her age in hours, so phototherapy is not indicated, and making jaundice the target distracts from the sodium and the feeding problem. Jaundice in this setting is largely a consequence of poor intake and improves as hydration and feeding improve. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on neonatal jaundice)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on neonatal jaundice

options.text: Perform a full septic screen with lumbar puncture and start intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin after cultures
options.rationale: A septic screen is mandatory in a lethargic neonate when the cause is not evident, but here the lethargy is fully explained by a documented 13 per cent weight loss with hypernatraemia, she is afebrile with a normal C reactive protein, and the feeding history identifies the mechanism. Cultures and antibiotics remain a low threshold addition if she does not improve with rehydration. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on febrile and unwell neonates)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on febrile and unwell neonates

explanation.summary: Hypernatraemic dehydration in the first week of life is almost always a lactation problem rather than a disease of the infant, arising when attachment difficulties or nipple trauma limit milk transfer before the milk supply is established. Weight loss beyond about ten per cent of birthweight, fewer than four wet nappies a day after day four, and persistent dark stools beyond day four are the practical warning signs. The clinical picture is deceptive because intravascular volume is relatively preserved in hypernatraemia, so the infant can look less unwell than the sodium suggests, and doughy skin with irritability or lethargy is more typical than shock. Correction is deliberately slow, with isotonic fluid and frequent electrolyte monitoring, because rapid falls in serum sodium cause cerebral oedema and seizures. Skilled lactation support is part of the treatment and not an afterthought, since most mothers can continue to breastfeed successfully once attachment is corrected and supply is supported.
key_points: Weight loss over ten per cent with lethargy and reduced wet nappies in the first week points to inadequate milk transfer.
Hypernatraemia preserves intravascular volume, so the infant may look better than the biochemistry suggests.
Correction uses isotonic fluid with a target fall in sodium of no more than about 0.5 mmol/L per hour.
Hypotonic fluid or glucose boluses risk cerebral oedema and seizures during correction.
Lactation support addresses the underlying cause and preserves breastfeeding.
explanation.pearls: Serum sodium should be rechecked four hourly during correction, and if it is falling faster than about 0.5 mmol/L per hour the sodium content of the fluid is increased or the rate reduced rather than the fluid simply being stopped.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on dehydration
Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on intravenous fluids
Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on neonatal jaundice
Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on febrile and unwell neonates

subtopic_detail: Recurrent bone pain at multiple sites with sterile biopsy cultures and no response to prolonged antibiotics in an eleven year old
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing an eleven year old girl in the outpatient clinic. Nine months ago she developed pain and swelling over the left clavicle, and a magnetic resonance scan then showed marrow oedema with periosteal reaction. An open biopsy grew no organisms and histology was reported as non specific chronic inflammation, and she completed two weeks of intravenous flucloxacillin followed by four weeks of oral therapy.

The clavicular pain settled partially but returned after treatment stopped, and for the last three weeks she has had pain in the right lower thigh that wakes her at night and eases with ibuprofen. She has had no fevers or weight loss, she is growing along her centiles, and her skin is clear apart from a few scattered comedones.

data_table.Examination: Tender fusiform swelling over the medial left clavicle with no overlying warmth, erythema or discharging sinus, tenderness over the distal right femoral metaphysis with full painless range of movement at both hips and knees, no joint effusion or synovitis at any joint, normal gait, no lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly, no rash on palms or soles
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 7.8 x10^9/L (4.0 to 12.0) with neutrophils 4.2 x10^9/L, haemoglobin 118 g/L (115 to 155), platelets 318 x10^9/L (150 to 450), C reactive protein 11 mg/L (less than 5), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 34 mm/h (less than 15), lactate dehydrogenase within normal limits, blood cultures from the first admission and biopsy cultures reported as no growth after extended incubation, plain radiograph of the right femur showing a lucent metaphyseal lesion with sclerotic margins

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Recommence intravenous antibiotics through a peripherally inserted central catheter for a further six week course
options.rationale: Six weeks of appropriate antibiotics with sterile blood and biopsy cultures and a relapse on cessation is evidence against bacterial osteomyelitis rather than an argument for more of the same. Repeating the course commits her to line related risks while the underlying inflammatory process continues. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on bone and joint infection)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on bone and joint infection

options.text: Arrange whole body magnetic resonance imaging and refer her to a paediatric rheumatology service for assessment
options.rationale: Culture negative multifocal osteitis that relapses after antibiotics is the pattern of chronic non bacterial osteomyelitis, and whole body magnetic resonance imaging is the investigation that establishes multifocality by revealing clinically silent lesions, which both supports the diagnosis and provides a baseline for monitoring. Demonstrating symmetrical or clavicular and metaphyseal lesions without an infective focus moves care to rheumatology, where non steroidal anti inflammatory therapy is first line. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on chronic non bacterial osteomyelitis)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on chronic non bacterial osteomyelitis

options.text: Perform a bone marrow aspirate and trephine with cytogenetics urgently to exclude leukaemia or a small round cell tumour
options.rationale: Marrow examination is the correct move when there are cytopenias, blasts on the film, a raised lactate dehydrogenase, systemic symptoms or a soft tissue mass, whereas her counts, film and lactate dehydrogenase are unremarkable and a lesion was already biopsied nine months ago. Malignancy remains in the differential and is addressed by biopsy of a representative lesion if imaging is atypical, rather than by marrow sampling first. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on chronic non bacterial osteomyelitis)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on chronic non bacterial osteomyelitis

options.text: Request a technetium bone scan to map skeletal involvement and plan any further biopsy around the sites identified
options.rationale: Scintigraphy does detect additional lesions but delivers ionising radiation and is less sensitive than whole body magnetic resonance imaging for marrow oedema, particularly in the vertebrae where collapse is the complication that changes management. It is the fallback when magnetic resonance imaging is unavailable or not tolerated. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on chronic non bacterial osteomyelitis)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on chronic non bacterial osteomyelitis

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone daily for four weeks and review her symptoms and inflammatory markers at the end of the course
options.rationale: Corticosteroid will suppress symptoms in several of the conditions on this differential, including malignancy, and so obscures the diagnosis before it has been made. In established chronic non bacterial osteomyelitis the first line agent is a non steroidal anti inflammatory drug, with corticosteroid, bisphosphonate or tumour necrosis factor blockade reserved for refractory or spinal disease. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology

explanation.summary: Chronic non bacterial osteomyelitis, historically called chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis when multiple sites are involved, is an autoinflammatory bone disease of children with a median onset around ten years of age. It characteristically affects the metaphyses of long bones, the clavicle, the pelvis and the vertebrae, produces pain that is often worse at night, and is accompanied by only modest elevation of inflammatory markers. The diagnostic difficulty is that each individual lesion mimics subacute bacterial osteomyelitis or a bone tumour, so children commonly receive prolonged antibiotics before the multifocal, culture negative, relapsing pattern is recognised. Whole body magnetic resonance imaging is central because clinically silent lesions are present in most children and their distribution, particularly symmetrical metaphyseal or clavicular involvement, supports the diagnosis while also identifying vertebral lesions at risk of collapse. Treatment begins with non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs, which control around half of cases, with bisphosphonates favoured for spinal disease and tumour necrosis factor inhibitors for refractory disease, and associated conditions such as palmoplantar pustulosis, severe acne and inflammatory bowel disease are sought.
key_points: Relapse after an adequate antibiotic course with sterile cultures is the observation that redirects the diagnosis away from bacterial osteomyelitis.
Clavicular and metaphyseal lesions with night pain and modestly raised inflammatory markers are the typical pattern.
Whole body magnetic resonance imaging reveals clinically silent lesions, confirms multifocality and identifies vertebral involvement.
Biopsy remains necessary for unifocal or atypical disease because malignancy cannot be excluded on imaging alone.
Non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs are first line, with bisphosphonates for spinal lesions and biologics for refractory disease.
explanation.pearls: Vertebral involvement is the reason whole body imaging is preferred over targeted scans, because vertebra plana from an undetected spinal lesion causes permanent deformity and is the finding that moves treatment straight to a bisphosphonate such as pamidronate rather than a trial of naproxen.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on chronic non bacterial osteomyelitis
Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on bone and joint infection
